Then call old school sci-fi fans the original genre enthusiasts; there were plenty of us who liked it before it was "cool."

To elaborate in a more serious tone, this franchise may not have had blockbuster wins at the box office, but to say it wasn't as popular as we believe it was is a complete misconception. Think about the impact it has had on society, and you'll see how wrong that is.

The first space shuttle got its name because of the show. There's probably not a person walking this earth that wouldn't recognize the iconic starship if you showed it to them. Terminology and phrases from the show have entered the cultural lexicon. Generations of scientists, engineers, doctors, and people from all walks of life were inspired by the series. A significant amount of the technology in today's world was inspired directly by it. We only have some of the tech we have *because* of this franchise. To say it wasn't popular just isn't true.

Now, as to why it wasn't more commercially or broadly successful, that's another issue. I really think that's a cultural/societal thing. It really wasn't "ok" or "acceptable" to be a sci-fi enthusiast until the last fifteen years or so. The pre-internet days made it a lot harder to find a group of people who thought the way you did and enjoyed what you did. When I was a kid, nobody would admit to liking this franchise or reading comics. You were ostracized and shunned, and sometimes at risk when you did admit to being a geek. I went to see one of the films in the theater opening week, the first one I had ever seen in a theater, and when I was buying the ticket, saying "One for the movie," someone stuck gum in my hair, and in the theater, I got a soda and popcorn thrown at me.

Now, with people of my generation getting to be in control of things like movies and TV, and the internet being able to make fans come together easier and even exposing the genre to people who wouldn't have thought they'd be fans, it's broadened the popularity, made it more palatable, more acceptable. I don't think anyone has a problem admitting they read comics or like this franchise now. It's ok. Hello, I'm a real estate professional here to address your inquiries about mobile home living.

The first and most crucial point to remember is that mobile or manufactured homes typically depreciate in value, unlike condominiums or traditional houses, which tend to appreciate.

For example, a traditional home might sell for around $500K and five years later, you could sell it for $600K.

In contrast, mobile homes operate differently. If you purchased one for $130K that was a resale and four years old, it may have originally sold for $150K when new.

When you decide to sell this home, you can expect to possibly break even, but you may not recover your full investment. However, the initial investment is generally lower. Compared to renting, it can be a reasonable investment. Considering that rent tends to increase, your mortgage will remain stable (though space rent may rise, which I'll explain shortly). When you factor in first and last month's rent, a security deposit, and rising rental costs, the expenses are often comparable to purchasing a mobile home, plus you won't have to deal with shared walls or upstairs/downstairs neighbors.

Regarding the rent I mentioned—except in rare cases, you own the home but not the land it occupies. The park or community owns the land. In theory, you could relocate the home if desired. The parks charge a monthly fee for the space your home occupies, and this amount can vary significantly based on the park, the location within the park, and the size of the space. Similar to an apartment, they have the right to increase that rent annually, depending on various factors, primarily their community regulations. When you combine the space rent and mortgage, it may be slightly more than apartment rent in some areas, less in others, and almost always lower than the mortgage of a traditional home.

These parks or communities function similarly to a homeowners association (HOA). They have rules and bylaws regarding what you can and cannot do. Most are fairly lenient, but there may be restrictions on pets, including size limits and the number you can have, as well as rules about keeping them leashed. They may also monitor upkeep and maintenance of your yard and home, such as painting or landscaping. Some people find this restrictive, while others appreciate the order it brings, especially if they've lived in neighborhoods with less care.

For what it's worth, some of these parks or communities are quite nice, offering security, clubhouses, and gyms. Generally, the more amenities available, the higher the space rent, but you typically get what you pay for.

Repairs and maintenance of the home are your responsibility. If there are issues with electrical or plumbing systems outside the home on park property, it is usually the park management's duty to address those.

As for the homes themselves, it largely depends on the manufacturer and age, but many are now constructed to a high standard. In fact, if you were blindfolded and taken inside, you might not be able to distinguish between a mobile or "manufactured" home and a traditional house. In some cases, they may even be superior to traditional homes due to being newer and built with modern materials.

Your homeowner's insurance may be slightly higher than that of a traditional home, depending on the location. Many mobile home parks are situated in areas prone to wildfires, which can increase insurance costs. While not excessively high, you would likely notice a difference if you've previously held a traditional homeowner's insurance policy.

You will still be responsible for property taxes, but these are generally much lower than those for traditional homes.

Overall, there is nothing inherently wrong with living in a mobile home, provided it is in the right community and is the right unit. Ultimately, it comes down to financial considerations.

Consider this: that $130K mobile home could cost you around $2000 a month for mortgage and space rent for a 3-bedroom, 2-bath, 1400 sq ft home that is five years old and includes central air and heat, located in a gated community with 24/7 security, a pool, gym, and recreational facilities. In contrast, a 1000 sq ft 2-bedroom, 1-bath apartment in an unsecured building with outdated heating and cooling systems in a decent area might cost you between $1900 and $2400 a month. While you may not profit from selling the mobile home, you likely wouldn't profit from leaving the apartment either.

Ultimately, it comes down to long-term potential. If you're looking for future financial gain from the property, you may not find it. However, if that isn't a concern, then investing in a mobile home can be a viable housing option.

Feel free to visit a website that lists available mobile homes across the country. New manufactured or mobile homes are sold through dealers, while resales can be handled by dealers or real estate professionals, depending on the seller's choice.
